summary: A designer and a critic per channel create and refine each of the 13 profile pictures and banners at real YouTube sizes, then an art director checks all 13 together for clashes and gets them fixed
logs: Resume: 27 of the journal's 27 saved results served from cache. Call 30 and every call after it run fresh, not from cache: it has no saved result (it or a call before it changed through a script edit, a reorder or different args, an earlier resume re-ran it without finishing, or the earlier run never started it).

design.idea: The mark is a stick figure whose head is a gold coin, so one shape does two jobs. That plays on "economy of means" (the most effect from the fewest strokes) and on "means" as money. The figure's arms are one straight line rising up and to the right. In the banner that arm presents the name, and behind it sits a faint graph-paper chart with a compound-growth curve and a gold coin ring at each doubling, taken from the channel's first script about compound interest and the Rule of 72.
design.palette: bg #14523A (deep banknote/chalkboard green), fg #F7F3E3 (chalk cream; name contrast 8.2:1), ac #F5C542 (coin gold; tagline contrast 5.6:1). Font: Inter Display, weight 800, letter-spacing -0.02em. markScale 0.72.
design.self_critique: Before this, the design was a thin-stroke figure on cream, which disappeared on YouTube's white background and smudged at 32 px. Ideas explored before building: (1) a coin-head figure; (2) the cent sign with a stick figure as its bar; (3) one line that is both a figure and a rising chart; (4) three stacked bars making an E. On contact sheets I also tried several poses: arms raised in a V (generic "yay" icon), arms out straight (reads as a female symbol or restroom icon), a star-jump X, and a single diagonal arm. On the proof sheet I fixed: thin strokes (now 12 units); a figure that was too big and sat to the left; an arm that touched or crowded the coin head; arms joining near the waist; the neck's round end poking into the coin (the coin is now drawn on top); muddy olive coin dots in the backdrop (now gold rings); and the curve clipping the phone view's corner (now about 27 px below the safe area). Weaknesses that remain: a stick figure is a common motif, so ownability rests on the coin head plus the green-and-gold colours. The coin's rim ring only shows from about 98 px up; at 32 px the head is a plain gold dot. The raised arm passes about 4 units from the coin, so at 32 px they nearly merge, though the colour change keeps them apart. The left half of the desktop view is sparse (grid and one axis line only). Green-and-gold is a familiar money pairing, and channel 2 also uses a gold accent, though on near-black rather than green.

design.idea: The mark is a classical temple front, the façade banks and holding companies hide behind and the Greek home of hubris. Its gold pediment is tipping, and its three columns get shorter left to right, so the same shape also reads as a falling bar chart: the "Holdings" stands proud and the "Hubris" brings it down. The banner backdrop is engraving from a share certificate: guilloche rope bands with ruled borders across the top and bottom of the TV view, and two seal medallions either side of the name on desktop.
design.palette: Banker's green and brass. Background #112A21 (deep bottle green), name #F2ECDD (warm ivory, 12.9:1 on the background), accent #D8A94E (brass gold, 7.05:1). No other channel in the portfolio has a green background. Name set in Caladea Bold (weight 700, spacing 0).
design.self_critique:
Ideas sketched first: (1) a tipping temple whose columns step down like a falling chart, (2) a top-heavy stack of slabs with a gold top block sliding off, (3) an H monogram whose right stem leans out, (4) an Icarus coin with a melting wing, (5) a crown slipping off a plinth. I rendered 1-3 side by side at 32-176 px. The stack read as a generic menu or filter icon. The H was bold but only said the initials. The temple was the only one that spoke to both words of the name, and it still reads at 32 px, so I built that.

Proof-sheet passes:
- Pass 1: the tilt was too gentle and the mark sat off-centre.
- Pass 2: steeper tilt (20 degrees) and a centred bounding box. The first backdrop's frame left stray vertical lines in the desktop view and the bands ended in arrow points.
- Pass 3: bands now run edge to edge between double rules, and the background green is richer.
- Pass 4: the rosettes had a bright pinpoint centre.
- Pass 5: tried an open-centre ring, plus a taller pediment so it reads as a temple.
- Pass 6: chunkier columns and base, markScale 0.7, rosettes became seals with an inner rule.

Remaining weaknesses:
- A temple front is a familiar "bank" pictogram. Only the tilt and the stepped columns make it ownable.
- At 32 px the pediment reads as a gold wedge more than a triangle.
- On desktop the two seals can read faintly as a pair of rings.
- The backdrop is about 17 KB of SVG.

Important finding: channels.json gives this channel the font "Bitstream Charter", which on this machine is a Type1 .pfb font. Chromium can't use it, so the shipped banner silently fell back to a sans-serif. I switched to Caladea, a TrueType serif. Channels 5 (Ink Tectonics) and 6 (Chamberstick) also list Bitstream Charter and will hit the same fallback.

design.idea: The mark is a pilcrow (¶, the typesetter's paragraph sign) whose bowl is half a gear. It reads the name in both halves: the ¶ stands for "legible" (plain written words) and the gear for "machines", so the two become one shape. On the banner, the name sits on a type designer's guide lines (cap height, x-height, a lime baseline ending in a circuit-style dot, and descender), set on blueprint graph paper with drafted meshing gears in the TV corners: type and machines drawn with the same instruments.
design.palette: bg #1C34A8 (cobalt / blueprint blue), fg #F5F8FF (cool white), ac #D2F55A (highlighter lime). Name on bg is 9.4:1 and tagline on bg is 8.0:1. No other channel in the portfolio uses a saturated mid-tone background; the others are near-black, dark green, plum, slate, cream, parchment, off-white or peach. Name in Inter Display 800 at -0.02em.
design.self_critique: Concepts I sketched on paper and rejected: a see-through glass-box cube (the black box opened), too generic and a tangle of lines at 32px; spectacles made of cogs, which looks steampunk, is too wide for a circle and gets fuzzy; a Snellen tumbling-E used as a chip with legs, which reads as a comb or the Cyrillic letter Ш; and a cursive "l" drawn by a circuit trace, too soft. Two I rendered and dropped: a pilcrow with a power cord, where the cord read as a question-mark hook, and a pilcrow with a circuit trace, which read as a joystick. The final half-gear pilcrow is one silhouette and holds up at 48 and 32px: a lime toothed bowl beside white stems. Remaining weaknesses: (1) The ¶ only reads as ¶ to people who know the symbol. Others will see "gear + Π/π", which is still on-topic but loses half the pun. (2) The banner gears are classic blueprint imagery, and the corner pairs are mirrored copies, so the TV view is tidy rather than surprising. (3) The guide lines are placed from Inter Display's metrics at the current 104px name size and layout in art.mjs (baseline y≈723.5), so they will drift if art.mjs changes the name size or position. (4) The gears sit only in the TV-only corners and the guide lines stop 40px short of the mark and name, so desktop and phone show just graph paper and the guide lines. That is calm and legible but plain on the far sides of the desktop view. No changes outside design/ch-3.json; the preview images in design/previews/ were rewritten by the preview script.

design.idea: The mark is the A of "Awe" drawn as a pair of drafting dividers. Their hinge is a lavender moon and their crossbar is the arc that marks an angle, so the same lines form the parallax triangle astronomers use to measure the distance to a star. The banner turns the whole sky into a graduated dial, a 360-degree ring with tick marks that frames the name. Behind it sit a faint star field, celestial hour lines, and two pairs of stars with drafting dimension lines between them: the stars, measured.
design.palette: bg #1B1560 (deep indigo; no other channel in the portfolio uses violet), fg #F4F1FF (name 14.3:1 on bg), ac #B4A7FF (lavender moon and tagline, 7.5:1 on bg). Name in Inter Display 700 at -0.01em; markScale 0.75; same background for picture and banner.
design.self_critique:
I tried 18 marks: a ruler-ring Saturn (read as a dumbbell), a planet on a dimension bar (read as a person), protractors sighting a moon (read as a gauge or joystick), a ruler exclamation mark, calipers (read as a claw machine), a notched crescent (generic), a dotted distance line and an angle of elevation (read as a figure in a chair), and several parallax As. I kept the parallax A because it is the only one that reads the name itself: Awe (the A), measured (dividers and an angle arc).

Weak points:
- At 32 px it reads mainly as a bold A with a moon. The tapered legs that make it read as dividers only come through from about 48 px up.
- Drafting compasses are a common icon type, so the moon hinge, the curved crossbar and the indigo palette carry most of the ownability.
- On YouTube's dark theme the indigo disc is only about 1.2:1 against #0f0f0f, so the circle's edge is soft there. The mark itself stays high contrast.
- In the TV view, the two measured star pairs are faint and could pass for stray lines.
- The phone view shows only a few faint stars beyond the name; the dial is too big to fall inside it.

Fixed along the way:
- Thin legs at 32 px: thickened to 19 units, tapering to 7.
- Mark too small, then too tight to the circle: scale set to 0.75.
- Round arc-end knobs, then fussy wedge spurs, which made the mark look like a figure: the arc now ends flush inside the legs.
- Dimension lines crossing the dial: moved inside it, into the bands only a TV shows.
- A flat, empty phone and desktop view: added faint stars and longer ticks every 30 degrees, which point at the name in the desktop view.

design.idea: The mark is a single drop of ink split in two along a stepped fault: an ink half and a red half drifting apart, the way a plate boundary breaks across a map. "Ink" is the drop and "Tectonics" is the split and the slip, and the two colours make the drop look like two territories on a political map. The banner backs this up with an old world-map grid around a cleared title space, red-ink ridges with transform offsets and seafloor stripes, and an atlas border with alternating degree bars.
design.palette: Parchment #EFE3C8 background, iron-gall ink #221A13 for the name and mark (13.5:1 on the background), cinnabar red #A8321F for the accent and tagline (5.25:1). It is the portfolio's only warm-paper palette, and the name is set in DejaVu Serif bold.
design.self_critique: I tried five other mark ideas first: a zigzag crack, a single kink, a coastline fit, a one-step cut and a mirrored step. I chose the two-step even-width cut because it echoes the ridges in the banner and reads cleanly at 32 and 48 px, where the two colours carry it. At mid sizes the cut can read a little like an S or a lightning bolt. The cut is a polyline painted in the background colour (#EFE3C8), hard-coded, so it must change if bg or logoBg ever changes. The cleared title space keeps the name clean but leaves the phone view almost bare, with only faint grid lines at its corners. The ridges stay inside the world outline and outside the phone-safe centre; the generator script asserts this. One thing for other designers: the channel's original font, Bitstream Charter, is installed only as Type1 files, which Chromium can't use, so the name silently fell back to a sans. That is why I switched to DejaVu Serif, which is not used elsewhere in the portfolio (ch-2 uses Caladea). Channels whose design keeps Charter (for example ch-6 in channels.json) will hit the same fallback. The backdrop is about 40 KB of paths, because the grid is sampled as polylines so the lines can stop at the title space. Generator kept at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Jachi/8146f71f-73d7-5544-b4d0-28b8048fbb36/scratchpad/gen5.py; final sheet at /home/user/Jachi/youtube-network/design/previews/ch-5-sheet.png.

design.idea: The mark draws a chamberstick, the short candle-holder people once carried up to bed. Its saucer is shaped like a crescent moon, and the finger ring on the side is what makes it a chamberstick rather than a plain candle. So the picture says the name itself, and the moon and the low wax-pooled candle say what the channel is for: quiet history at bedtime. On the banner, faint bands of candlelight spread out from the logo's flame, and on TVs a dark old town with a few lit windows sits along the bottom.
design.palette: Background aubergine #2A1C36, name in warm wax cream #F3E9D8, accent candle amber #F2B45A. Name on background 13.3:1. Tagline on background 8.7:1, and at least 7.3:1 measured on the rendered banner where the glow sits behind it. The name is set in FreeSerif at weight 400 with 0.015em spacing, a serif no other channel in the portfolio uses.
design.self_critique: I tried six ideas side by side (the original candle, a crescent dish, a three-quarter-view saucer, a C-shaped ring around a flame, an arched bedroom door, a looped handle) before picking the crescent dish with the finger ring. The first proof showed a real flaw: the narrow candle with a dot-like flame read as the letters "io". I fixed it with a wider, stubbier candle with a melted pool on top, and dropped the thin wick, so every part is now at least 8 units thick. In this final version the flame, cup and ring are all clear at 48 px. At 32 px the ring shrinks to a dot with a speck of a hole: it still reads as a candle with a handle, but the chamberstick detail is only fully clear from 48 px up. The left tip of the crescent is a sharp point that will soften when scaled down, and the weight leans slightly left because the candle sits left of the ring. The glow bands are deliberately stepped; YouTube's image compression may make that banding a little coarser. FreeSerif is calm and bookish but close to Times, so the name type is less distinctive than the mark. The town has a dome to suggest places outside Europe, but it still leans European. The glow is centred on where the flame sits for this exact name and font, so it would drift a little if art.mjs's banner layout changed. The town sits entirely below the desktop crop, so the desktop and phone views show only the logo, the name and the soft glow.

design.idea: The mark is a faceless rogue in a Victorian bowler hat posing for a booking photograph. He stands in front of three thick height-chart bars and holds a dark slate at his chest, so the "rogue" is the historic con man or thief and "of record" is the police photograph that put him on file. The banner keeps the same idea: a faint booking-room height chart fills the TV view, with ruler ticks down both edges. The name is set in a bold typewriter face, like a typed police report, and reads as told from the record.
design.palette: Oxblood #4A161A, the red leather of old court and police ledgers (background). Bone #F4EADB, the ledger page (name and figure, 12.4:1). Ledger-rule blue #A9C8E6 (accent: height bars, backdrop rules and tagline, 8.5:1). No other channel uses a red background, and no other channel uses this cool blue on warm red. It also stays clear of the black-and-red default of the crime trio (11-13).
design.self_critique:
Three ideas were drawn and rendered. (A) The bowler-hat rogue against a height chart. (B) A clerk's rubber-stamp ring around a domino mask, which read as an infinity sign or glasses at 32 px, so I dropped it. (C) Ledger rules with one rule knocked out of line, which read as the letter Z or a menu icon, so I dropped it. A was refined over five proof sheets:
- The first hat read as a cowboy or ranger hat. I narrowed the brim to about 1.4 times the dome, joined the dome to the brim and dropped the rakish tilt.
- I added the dark booking slate so it stops looking like a generic user icon.
- I moved the bars so the occlusion cuts are clean, with no nubs at the brim tips.
- I centred the figure vertically, raised the mark scale to 0.78 and thickened the bars to 10 units for the 32 px circle.
- I pulled the bars in from the rim so there is breathing room at 176 px.

At 32 px it reads as a hatted figure against lines with a dark slate. At 48 px and up it is clearly a mugshot.

Remaining weaknesses:
- At 32 px the pale-blue bars and the bone figure sit close in lightness. The 9-unit halo keeps them apart, but it is the busiest part of the mark.
- A bust silhouette is a familiar icon form. The bowler, the slate and the height chart are what make it ownable.
- The monospace name has wide word gaps. That is intended (the typewritten-report feel), but it is less tight than a sans.

Font issue for the other designers: "Courier 10 Pitch" and "Bitstream Charter" are Type1 (.pfb) fonts that Chromium does not load. They silently fall back to a sans-serif, so I used FreeMono Bold instead. It is installed with the same GNU FreeFont package as FreeSans and FreeSerif, and it renders correctly.

Only design/ch-7.json was written. The preview images in design/previews/ were regenerated by preview.mjs.

design.idea: A navy contract page has its fine print dimmed, and an orange sign-here flag sticks out past the edge, pointing at the one bright line where you sign. The flag reads the HERE in Hereby and the moment you hereby agree, and the dimmed print with one clear line stands for Explained, which is the channel's promise to point at the part that matters. I weighed three other ideas on paper first: a section sign uncoiling into a straight line, a notary seal with an H, and an X on a signature line. I dropped them because they were generic to law, or (the X) looked like a close button at 32 px.
design.palette: bg #F4F5F1 (cool paper), fg #14213D (blue-black signature ink), ac #B04A00 (burnt-orange sign-here flag). Name on bg 14.6:1, tagline on bg 5.0:1. No other channel uses a light paper background with navy and orange. Ch-5's parchment and brick red differ in hue (orange about 25 degrees against red about 8). Name font is FreeSans 700 at -0.01em, a plain Helvetica-like face that no other channel uses. Bitstream Charter was tried first, but it is a Type 1 font that Chromium can't load, so it fell back to a default sans.
design.self_critique: Five proof-sheet rounds, after three side-by-side variant sheets for the mark. Changes along the way: the stubby flag read as a price tag, so it became a long, slim sign-here flag reaching past the page edge. The two text lines were dimmed so the signature line and flag lead at 32 px. A navy avatar background lost to the paper one, which keeps the avatar and the banner consistent. Mark scale went up to 0.73. The accent was darkened from #B84E00 (4.65:1) to #B04A00 (5.0:1). In the banner, the boxy fine-print blocks became a full two-column contract page that fades toward the name, so the phone view is completely clean and the desktop edges carry faint text. A signature line with a caption sits bottom right, with a faded sign-here flag stuck to the page edge. Two highlighter swipes mark the clauses a video would explain, and there is a folded top-right corner. Weaknesses: the page with a folded corner is a familiar document glyph, close in kind to generic file icons and to the Google Docs icon, so ownership rests on the orange flag and the navy-and-orange pair. On YouTube's white theme the paper circle's edge is faint, though the mark still reads at 32 and 48 px. At a glance the fine print can look a little like a loading-skeleton UI. The mark and backdrop use only g and path, there is no text in the backdrop, and the final preview exits 0.

design.idea: A thick round cloister arch with three staggered streaks of rain falling inside it: the view from the covered walk out into weather, so it reads as both words of the name, and the uneven streaks also look like a quiet sound meter. The banner carries the same idea at full size. You look out through a stone arcade, with joints on the arches, dark piers and a low wall, at fine rain that thins out behind the name.
design.palette: Wet slate #22323B background, pale stone #E7EDEB name and arch (11.2:1), verdigris #86C5B6 accent for the rain and tagline (6.7:1). Name in Inter Display Regular (400) at +0.01em, which is calm and holds up at phone size. No other channel uses this cool slate with verdigris.
design.self_critique: I sketched three ideas: an arch with rain, an arch standing on a sill, and a raindrop with an arched door cut into it. I dropped the sill version because it reads as a headstone, and the raindrop because it looks cute and its door disappears at 32 px. I chose the arch with rain. Over later rounds I stopped the right streak touching the arch, widened the inside of the arch and staggered the streaks so they read as rain rather than an equaliser. I also removed crossing ring lines over the piers, replaced parapet joints that looked like a ruler with a single coping band, and added stone joints on the arch rings. Finally I changed the name from weight 300 to 400 for phones. What remains: at 32 px the three streaks nearly merge into one teal cluster, though the arch outline stays clear. The slate circle barely stands out from YouTube's dark background (1.45:1), so recognition there depends on the light arch. At a glance the mark can also be read as a lowercase n. On TV the low-wall strip at the bottom is plain, and the rain in the side bays clumps a little.

design.idea: The mark is an exclamation mark whose dot has rolled away. The bar still stands where it was, with an empty space below it, and the dot (in the accent colour) sits at the far end of the floor line, about to roll off. The "!" stands for the catastrophe and the runaway dot makes it a modest one: a small, deadpan mishap that also works as a tiny character with a grown-up bad day. The banner is a still, wide shot of an empty waiting room: a pendant lamp lighting an empty spot on a tiled floor, a wall clock reading a few minutes past nine, a door, and on the TV view a second accent dot quietly heading for the door.
design.palette: Background is a chalky sage-grey #D3D9C9, a muted, pale look taken from deadpan cinema. Foreground is ink #1E2320, 11.0:1 on the background. Accent is raspberry #9A2F4E, used for the tagline at 5.0:1 and for the dot. No other channel in the portfolio uses sage with raspberry. The name is set in Inter Display at weight 600 with -0.015em tracking, a weight no other channel uses. Bitstream Charter and Courier 10 Pitch are installed only as Type1 fonts, which Chromium can't draw, so neither was used.
design.self_critique: Ideas I considered first: a coffee mug lying in its spilled coffee, a small personal raincloud (too close to channel 9's rain), a knocked-over traffic cone, and several versions of the exclamation mark. Of those, I tried lying flat (it read as a megaphone), tipping over (it read as an italic "!") and dot-rolled-away (chosen). The first stubby bar read as a cup or tumbler. A sharper wedge that narrows to a rounded point fixed that. At 32 px the shape is clearly a "!" with a red dot beside it. The floor line is about 2.5 px there, which is thin but visible. To keep the line clear of the circle's edge it is shorter, and the mark scale is 0.77. Without colour the joke loses some of its punch, because the moved dot relies on the accent. Against YouTube's white background the pale sage circle has fairly little edge contrast, though the mark itself stays strong. The banner backdrop uses a few hard-coded #FFFFFF fills (the light pool and the clock face) next to currentColor and the accent. The backdrop shows a clock and a door but no text. The far-off dot by the door is a deliberate story gag that some viewers may take for a stray mark. The circle sizes and the desktop and phone views now look clean. The TV view has a smooth vignette after an earlier version showed visible bands.

design.idea: A key whose bow is a speech balloon: the person who talked was the key that opened the case, a visual play on 'key witness'. It reads the name directly ('someone talked' = the balloon, 'until' = the moment it unlocked everything), and the banner tells the same story as a multitrack wiretap where every track is silent room tone until, just after the playhead, the one track level with the name starts talking.
design.palette: Night asphalt navy bg #0F1820, warm off-white fg #F2ECE2 (15.3:1), sodium-streetlight orange accent #F08A24 (7.1:1 on bg). This is the only navy-and-orange palette in the portfolio, and it keeps clear of channel 7's oxblood red.
design.self_critique:
Ideas I sketched before building: (1) the key-witness key with a balloon bow, (2) a flat line that bursts into a waveform, (3) a row of dots for the crew with one turning into a balloon, (4) a balloon behind bars. I dropped (4) because it reads as 'free speech jailed'. I dropped (3) because its detail disappears at 32 px. I dropped (2) because audio waveforms are a generic podcast look, and kept that idea for the banner instead.

How the mark changed: v1 was a rounded-rectangle balloon bow with a hole, and the hole made it look like a bird's eye. Taking the hole out made the balloon read clearly. But a rectangular body with a horizontal blade and a down-left tail could be glimpsed as a pistol, which is wrong for a channel that promises not to glamorise crime. A round bow fixed that, because round bow plus blade is the classic key silhouette. After that I made the tail wider and curved it like a comic balloon tail, raised markScale to 0.78, and nudged the mark about 1.5 units right and 1 unit down so its centre sits between its bounding box and its weight. At 32 px it reads as an orange balloon-key, but the gap between the two teeth blurs into one block. The key still reads; only the second tooth is lost.

Font: Bitstream Charter and Courier 10 Pitch are Type 1 fonts that Chromium silently can't use (channel 2's original Charter fell back to sans the same way). I chose DejaVu Sans Bold at -0.02em. No other channel uses it, and it gives a sturdy, municipal, street-level look, though it's a little plain next to a true cinematic title face.

Banner: I moved the centre track's gap out to x 470-2090 so phones show no stray dots, and lowered the talking burst to 0.38 opacity. On desktop the burst at the right edge is still noticeable; that's on purpose but it does compete slightly. On TV the silent tracks read as fine dotted rules rather than obvious waveforms until you look closely. Channels 12 and 13 hadn't been designed yet, so check their palettes against navy and orange when they are.

design.idea: The mark is a crooked equals sign. The top bar is a straight printed rule in paper white, and the lower bar is a highlighter-yellow stroke with chiselled ends, knocked 9 degrees off level, so it reads as a sum that doesn't balance, the bottom line fiddled and flagged by an investigator: "crooked" plus "arithmetic" in two shapes. The banner backdrop shows the same story as a faint ledger. Columns of grouped figures run down both sides, and a thin yellow pen trail underlines the figures being followed, runs down the gutter and ends on an accountant's double rule under a total whose lower line is crooked, which echoes the mark.
design.palette: bg #1C1D20 (graphite), fg #F4F2EA (paper white), ac #EDE04A (highlighter yellow). Name on background 15.0:1, tagline (accent on background) 12.3:1. No other channel uses a neutral graphite background with a lemon accent: ch-1's gold is on green, ch-2's on deep green, and ch-11 is orange on blue-black. Font: Inter 800, letter-spacing -0.03em.
design.self_critique: Ideas I considered on paper: (1) the crooked equals, which I chose; (2) a calculator's seven-segment digit with one segment knocked askew, rejected because seven parts blur at 32px; (3) a plus sign with one bent arm, rejected because it can look like a medical cross or worse; (4) a ledger column with a crooked total rule, which the equals already distils and which the backdrop now uses. What each sheet fixed: v1 bars were too thin and the mark too small, and the diagonal money trail read like a line chart. v2 made the bars thicker and the trail right-angled. v3 compared JetBrains Mono with Inter. The mono felt like a coding channel and was too close to ch-7's mono, so I kept Inter 800. That sheet also dropped a stepped vignette that showed bands and replaced murky olive highlight boxes. v4 changed those to yellow pen underlines and added the crooked double rule. v5 and v6 used thinner bars with a wider gap so the mark reads as "=" rather than slabs, and shorter bars at markScale 0.9 so it fills the circle. v7 faded the centre texture so it doesn't look like loading placeholders. v8 tightened the gap and softened the chisel so the two bars read as one sign at 32px. Remaining weaknesses: the mark is wide and short, so the circle has empty space above and below. At 220px in the banner it looks a little slight next to the 104px name. Yellow at low opacity on graphite turns olive, so the backdrop accents are kept thin, which makes them very quiet on a TV. A plain "=" can't be made fully distinctive; what makes it this channel's is the tilt plus the highlighter colour.

design.idea: The mark is a classical front doorcase: an open pediment over a cream door left ajar, with a blade of emerald light at the gap. The doorcase is the "Respectable" front door, and the crack of light is the crime going on behind it, word for word the tagline's "behind respectable doors". The banner extends this into a mahogany-panelled wall (the respectable front). The name sits in its central plaque, and on the far left one panel is really a concealed door whose seam glows green.
design.palette: Mahogany #2B1712 (background), ivory #F3EADB (name and mark), emerald #3CC48F (the light and the tagline): the colours of a banker's lamp in a panelled boardroom. Name on background 14.3:1, tagline on background 7.7:1. No other channel uses a brown background or an emerald accent.
